I recently set out on a journey to build a Python script that tracks our AI API costs across four different providers using DeepSeek. After a week of late-night debugging (thanks to some interesting AI 'hallucinations'), I managed to save my team about $2,000 per month in unnecessary spending. Curious about how it all unfolded? Let me share my experience!

1. The Problem That Started It All

So, here's the deal: our team was burning through AI API credits faster than I could keep track. We had engineers using OpenAI for various tasks, a research project leveraging Anthropic Claude, my own experiments with DeepSeek, and the data team diving into Google's Gemini. The end result? Financial chaos!

Invoices were arriving in different formats at totally unpredictable times, and when I finally added everything up, I was shocked $4,700 per month! Almost half of that went to premium models for tasks that really didn't need them.

What I needed was a command-line tool that could:
1. Pull usage data from all four providers
2. Normalize costs into a single view
3. Identify our most expensive models
4. Generate a simple HTML dashboard for the team

This felt like a job for DeepSeek! While I only have basic Python skills, I thought having AI handle the tedious work of wiring together four different API SDKs with authentication and cost normalization was a smart move.

2. Building the Tracker with DeepSeek

I decided to craft a detailed prompt for DeepSeek, hoping to generate a solid foundation to build upon:

bash

To my surprise, DeepSeek generated about 800 lines of code using standard libraries like  and . It even included a cute animated spinner for data fetching. I thought, "This is too good to be true!" 

3. Where the AI Code Fell Apart

But when I ran  with my actual API keys, the issues began to surface.

Imaginary API Endpoints

First, I discovered that DeepSeek had completely fabricated OpenAI's usage API endpoint:
bash
This URL doesn't exist! OpenAI's usage data actually comes from their billing dashboard API or CSV exports. The AI generated something that looked plausible but was purely fictional.

Cost Calculation Errors

Then, I noticed that the script assumed all providers used the same pricing formulas. In reality, it was way more complicated:
Anthropic rounds token counts per request
Google returns costs in micros (millionths of a cent)
DeepSeek provides token counts but no cost data

Pagination Problems

When I tested it with real production data, it only captured the most recent 100 records from each provider. Each API handles pagination differently, which the AI code overlooked completely:
OpenAI uses cursor-based pagination
Anthropic uses offsets
Google uses page tokens
DeepSeek uses limit/offset

Rate Limit Chaos

With 12 API keys across four providers, the script's basic  approach didn't cut it. We quickly hit:

The single retry attempt after 5 seconds was insufficient for our actual usage patterns.

4. The Fixes That Made It Work

After six evenings of debugging, here's what I changed:

API Endpoints (2 hours): I replaced all fictional endpoints with the real ones from each provider's documentation.

Cost Calculations (1 hour): I built provider-specific cost calculators with hardcoded pricing tables (as of June 2026) and added a  flag to keep them updated.

Pagination (2 hours): I implemented proper pagination for each provider using generator patterns to handle their different approaches.

Rate Limiting (1 hour): I swapped the basic sleep for a proper token-bucket system that respects each provider's limits and rotates through available keys.

Dashboard (30 minutes): I rewired the AI-generated HTML template to use our actual normalized cost data instead of the hallucinated numbers.

The final version consisted of three files:
 (600 lines) Main CLI
 (500 lines) Provider-specific logic
 (300 lines) HTML generation

Testing against 90 days of real usage showed costs within 3-5% of provider dashboards.

5. The Real Savings

With visibility into our costs, the waste became painfully clear:
OpenAI GPT-5: A forgotten background job using GPT-5 instead of GPT-4-mini $800/month
Anthropic Claude Opus: Research team using Opus when Sonnet would suffice $600/month
DeepSeek: Double-paying through a 30% markup aggregator $400/month
Google Gemini: Unlimited test accounts running expensive experiments $200/month

Total savings: around $2,000/month!

6. Lessons Learned

This project taught me some valuable lessons about working with AI-generated code:

1. AI can invent plausible-looking APIs That two-hour wild goose chase for a non-existent endpoint was a real eye-opener. The AI can be confidently wrong.

2. Pricing changes frequently Hardcoded cost tables can go stale fast. The  flag became essential.

3. Rate limiting can get complex quickly What works for one key may fail spectacularly with multiple. A proper token bucket system solved the issue.

4. Pagination is a silent killer Without proper handling, you'

## How We Built a Log Monitor with DeepSeek (Step-by-Step

**Pillar:** AI Automation Scripts

Our team built a Python log monitoring script using DeepSeek, but boy, did the generated code need some serious fixing. Let us walk you through our journey from messy log files to a working solution complete with the exact prompt you can use for your own experiments!

1. The Problem That Kept Us Up at Night

Every morning, our team found ourselves scrolling through , trying to spot new issues. Our servers were generating hundreds of errors overnight, and we needed a way to know when things went south quickly. The pattern was clear: if we saw more than three errors in a 5-minute window, we wanted an alert. 

What we needed was a lightweight Python script that could:
Tail the log file in real-time
Count errors in rolling windows
Send a ping to my Slack whenever the thresholds were crossed
Run smoothly on any Ubuntu box without heavy dependencies

After a week of coding manually, I thought, "Why not ask AI for help  So, I turned to DeepSeek to generate the complete workflow, hoping to learn how to prompt AI for real automation tasks.

2. My DeepSeek Prompt (and What Came Back)

I crafted a detailed prompt that covered everything from log parsing to sending Slack notifications. Here's exactly what I provided to DeepSeek:

bash

Surprisingly, DeepSeek returned 560 tokens (about 3.8KB) of polished code. It had colored output, used  properly, and even included daemon functionality. For comparison, OpenCode's output was more compact but completely messed up the sliding-window logic.

3. Where the AI Code Failed

The first red flag popped up when I ran the script on a clean VM:

powershell

Here were some other issues I stumbled upon:
1. The sliding-window logic reset after each check rather than maintaining state.
2. The webhook payload had non-serializable datetime objects.
3. OpenCode's version entirely omitted the webhook functionality.
4. Neither version properly handled missing dependencies.

The cost for using DeepSeek was minimal (around $0.0018 for the API call), but the debugging time? That really added up.

4. How I Fixed the AI's Code

I took DeepSeek's output as a starting point and made these key improvements:

1. Dependency checks I added clear error messages when  or  were missing.
2. Proper windowing I fixed the deque logic to maintain error counts across checks.
3. JSON fixes I converted datetimes to ISO strings before the webhook calls.
4. Graceful degradation Made colored output optional if  isn't available.
5. Better daemonizing Switched to  for proper PID file handling.
6. Robust logging Added log rotation to avoid disk bloat.

The final script runs in 0.32 seconds for initial load and uses minimal CPU (under 2% on a 2-core server).

5. Key Lessons Learned

1. AI is like a junior dev Great for first drafts but really needs careful review.
2. Test in clean environments What works on your dev machine might fail elsewhere.
3. Prompt specifically My detailed prompt helped, but I still had to add "check for missing packages."
4. Log everything Proper logging saved me hours of debugging.
5. Cost vs. quality DeepSeek's output was more useful despite the small cost.

The fixed script has been running smoothly on my production servers for a month now. It's not enterprise-grade (you'd likely want to add proper rate limiting and TLS verification for that), but it does solve my immediate problem.

## Core Web Vitals Failing? 7 Fixes to Save Rankings

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/core-web-vitals-fail-new-website-improve-lcp-inp-cls
**Published:** 2026-06-18

> If your new website fails Core Web Vitals before publishing, fix LCP, INP, and CLS now. Here are 7 urgent fixes to protect your rankings.

A Common Dilemma

So, you've just built your shiny new website, but it's failing Core Web Vitals? That can be pretty frustrating, right? If you're scratching your head wondering how to tackle this, you're not alone. The good news is that there are some actionable steps you can take to improve your site's performance before it goes live.

Here's What Our Team Found

Core Web Vitals measure how users experience your website. They assess how quickly the main content loads, how responsive the page is to user interactions, and how stable the layout is while loading. Specifically, we're looking at three key metrics: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS).

If your site is struggling, it's often due to large images, slow server responses, or layout shifts. Testing tools like PageSpeed Insights can help you pinpoint these issues. 

Step-by-Step Breakdown

Here's a friendly guide to help you tackle these Core Web Vital issues. Let's dive in!

1. Test Your URL: Start by testing the exact URL you plan to publish on PageSpeed Insights. It'll give you a clear picture of LCP, INP, and CLS scores, along with other important metrics. Our team often jots these down to track our progress.

2. Make the Staging Site Accessible: If your staging site is password-protected, consider temporarily lifting the restrictions so testing tools can access it. This can often be adjusted in your site's settings.

3. Optimize Your Hero Image: Your hero image can significantly impact LCP. Check the image size and format. Aim for a smaller size (around 120-220 KB for desktop and 60-140 KB for mobile) and consider using formats like WebP or AVIF for better compression.

4. Avoid Lazy Loading for Key Images: Make sure your main hero image isn't set to lazy load. This can delay its appearance and negatively affect LCP. Set the width and height attributes for the image to avoid layout shifts.

5. Streamline CSS and JavaScript: Heavy scripts can block rendering. Use tools like Chrome's Lighthouse to identify which scripts can be deferred or removed. In WordPress, plugins can help manage this.

6. Eliminate Unnecessary Scripts: Review your plugins and third-party tools. Sometimes chat widgets or sliders can add significant loading time. Consider loading them after user interaction instead of on the initial page load.

7. Stabilize Your Layout: To reduce CLS, set width and height attributes for all images and reserve space for ads and embeds. This helps avoid content jumping around while the page loads.

8. Check Font Loading: If you're using custom fonts, ensure you're not loading too many font weights. Two should suffice for most sites. Use  in your CSS to ensure text appears promptly.

9. Simulate Real User Experience: Use Chrome DevTools to mimic how your site looks on mobile devices. Interact with the site to see if you notice any layout shifts or delays.

10. Retest After Changes: After making adjustments, go back to PageSpeed Insights to see how your changes have impacted your scores. Tackle one major issue at a time to track improvements accurately.

Limitations: This Won't Work If...

These tips might not solve your issues if your hosting server is slow, or if there's something blocking the test tools from accessing your site. If your Time to First Byte is over 800 milliseconds, you might need to look into better hosting or a closer CDN.

Deep Dive: Advanced Caching and Edge Delivery

If you've implemented all the front-end optimizations above and are still struggling to hit the elusive "Good" thresholds for LCP and INP, it's time to look at your infrastructure. Our team recently audited a high-traffic React application where the culprit wasn't unoptimized images, but rather server response times and main-thread blocking.

Implementing a Redis Object Cache

If your site relies on a database-heavy CMS (like WordPress or Drupal), database queries can severely bottleneck your Time to First Byte (TTFB), which directly delays your LCP. We deployed Redis as an in-memory object cache to store the results of complex queries. 

By adding the Redis extension to our PHP configuration and enabling it via our CMS framework, we reduced TTFB from 600ms to a consistent 120ms.

bash

Edge Computing for Dynamic Content

To further drive down LCP for global users, we moved HTML rendering to the edge using Cloudflare Workers. Instead of routing every request back to the origin server in New York, we cached the static shell of our pages at the edge node nearest to the user. 

This strategy ensures that the primary HTML document arrives almost instantly, allowing the browser's preload scanner to discover critical assets (like CSS and the LCP image) much earlier in the page lifecycle.

What's Your Take?
Our team is always curious to hear how others tackle these issues. Have you faced challenges with Core Web Vitals? What strategies have worked for you? Let's chat in the comments!

References & Further Rea

## Discovered - Currently Not Indexed: How to Fix GSC Cra

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/sitemap-submitted-but-pages-undiscovered-robotstxt-check
**Published:** 2026-06-18

> Your sitemap says submitted successfully but pages stay undiscovered? Check robots.txt, internal links, and canonicals to fix it.

Direct Answer: How to Sitemap Submitted but Pages Stay Undiscovered? (Step-by-Step)
Have you ever submitted a sitemap only to find that some pages remain undiscovered? You're not alone! Just because your sitemap shows as 'submitted successfully' doesn't guarantee that Google will index every page. Think of it more like a suggestion rather than a command. In our team's experience, the first things to look at are robots.txt, weak internal links, and canonical tags that might be misdirecting Google. If those look good, then it's worth checking page quality, redirects, noindex tags, and any server response issues.

1. Explanation

This can be a bit confusing when you're navigating Google Search Console. You submit your XML sitemap, Google accepts it, and everything seems okay. But then you check the Pages report and find URLs marked as Crawled currently not indexed, Discovered currently not indexed, or Excluded by 'noindex' tag.

The main purpose of a sitemap is to inform Google about the existence of your URLs and how often they're updated. It doesn't force Google to crawl, index, or rank them. Google's own documentation explains this well: Sitemaps overview.

When a page stays undiscovered, it could be for a few common reasons. Google may find the URL in the sitemap but then hit a wall with your robots.txt file. If a page lacks internal links, Google might see it as isolated. There could also be a canonical tag pointing to another URL, which tells Google to ignore the page you want indexed.

This issue often pops up with newly published blog posts, product listings, category pages, and promotional landing pages. The sitemap may look fine, but if the page isn't well-linked from your homepage or related posts, or if it has a canonical tag that's just wrong, it can be problematic. So, our team likes to think of sitemap status as a starting point in troubleshooting, not the final answer.

2. When This Fix Works

This fix is effective when Google can technically access the page but isn't crawling it due to mixed messages from your site. For instance, if your sitemap includes , but your robots.txt file blocks , Google sees the URL, checks the rules, and then decides to exclude it from crawling.

It can also help when pages lack internal links. If you've got a new page in your sitemap that isn't linked from key pages like your homepage or a related post, it may be sitting in a weak discovery state. From what our team has seen, adding just a couple of contextual links from relevant pages can really help Google understand that this page is part of your site.

It's also relevant when canonical tags are incorrect. A common issue, especially with WordPress, is when a canonical tag points to the homepage or some unrelated page. If that's the case, Google might just follow that signal and ignore your desired page.

3. When This Does NOT Work

However, this fix won't work if the page is considered thin, duplicated, or not valuable enough for Google to bother indexing. Simply having a sitemap won't make a low-value page worth crawling. Even if everything looks technically correct, Google might pass over a page with only a few words of duplicated content.

Also, if the URL returns an error (like 404, 410, 500, or even a soft 404), then your sitemap is pointing Google to a page that doesn't exist properly. You'll want to resolve the page's status first.

This approach won't fix ranking issues either. A page can be indexed but still rank poorly due to weak content or competition from stronger pages. For that, you'll need to focus on improving content and SEO, not just fixing the sitemap.

And if your website is brand new, it might just need some time. New sites often experience slower initial crawl rates from Google. Our team typically waits 2 to 6 weeks before making any judgments about crawl behavior, assuming the technical setup is correct.

4. Step-by-Step Instructions

1. Open Google Search Console and select your website property from the menu on the left.

2. Click on Sitemaps under the Indexing section. Check the submitted sitemap URL, like . If it's incorrect, remove it and submit the right one.

3. Open the Pages report under Indexing. Look for the affected URL in Discovered currently not indexed, Crawled currently not indexed, or Not found (404). If the page isn't listed, paste the exact URL in the inspection field and hit Enter.

4. Run the URL Inspection test for the affected page. Check if Google says the URL is available. If it says it's blocked by robots.txt, you'll want to check that next.

5. Test robots.txt using Google's official tool. Head to the robots.txt testing tool and enter your URL. If it's blocked, check your robots.txt file at .

6. Remove any rules that block the page or section you want indexed. For example, change  to a more specific rule, or remove it altogether if you want all blog posts crawled.

7. Check the live page for a noindex tag. In your browser, right-click on the page and select V

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO

**Published:** 2026-06-18

> If Google Search Console says your sitemap URLs are blocked by robots.txt, clean up your sitemap and resubmit it in GSC with this guide.

Direct Answer: How to Fix Sitemap URLs Blocked by Robots.txt
Have we ever found ourselves staring at Google Search Console, only to see that our sitemap URLs are blocked by robots.txt? That can be a real head-scratcher! But don't worry our team has some tips to help us clean up our sitemap and resubmit it. The main idea is to remove any URLs from our sitemap that aren't meant to be there, especially those that are blocked, duplicate, private, or non-canonical. After that, we might need to tweak our robots.txt file, but only if it's blocking a useful page by mistake. Then, we can test the affected URLs in Google Search Console and resubmit our sitemap. Simple enough, right?
1. Explanation

So, what's going on here? An XML sitemap is essentially a wish list for Googlebot it's a list of URLs we'd like Google to find. On the flip side, robots.txt is a set of rules that tells Googlebot what it can and cannot crawl on our site. If there's a match between a Disallow rule in robots.txt and a URL in our sitemap, Googlebot can't crawl that URL, even though it's listed in the sitemap. 

According to Google Search Central, these robots.txt rules dictate what Googlebot can crawl. 

This kind of issue can pop up after you've made some changes to your CMS, migrated your site, or updated an SEO plugin. Suddenly, your sitemap might start including unwanted pages like tag pages, author pages, or even old URLs that should be long gone. 

For instance, if your sitemap includes , but your robots.txt has this rule:

bash

Googlebot will be unable to crawl that URL. The fix? Just remove  from your sitemap. 

Another example is if you have a live page under , but robots.txt has:

bash

In this case, your sitemap might be fine, but robots.txt is too broad. You would want to edit robots.txt to allow Google to crawl your actual blog pages. 

If you're still setting things up, it's a good idea to start with the basics.

2. When This Fix Works

This approach works well when your sitemap includes pages you genuinely want Google to crawl, but robots.txt is mistakenly blocking them. For example, if you have a real service page at , but robots.txt says , that's a problem you can fix! 

It's also helpful if your sitemap has junk URLs things that should never be there, like tag pages or staging URLs. After a site migration, if your old sitemap still lists  while robots.txt blocks , cleaning up the sitemap can resolve that conflict. 

The best outcome occurs when you address both sides: removing unwanted sitemap URLs and correcting overly broad robots.txt rules.

3. When This Does NOT Work

Now, there are some situations where this fix won't be applicable. If a page is private and should remain that way like an admin page or internal file you'll want to keep the robots.txt rule and just remove it from the sitemap. 

Similarly, if a page has a noindex tag and you want it indexed, you'll need to remove that noindex tag first. If the server returns errors like 403, 401, or 500, that's a different issue altogether it's a server or permissions problem, not a sitemap conflict. 

And if the canonical URL points elsewhere, Google might ignore your submitted URL in favor of the canonical version. For issues like that, you might want to explore further.

Lastly, if your sitemap file itself is broken returning 404, 500, or invalid XML Google Search Console won't be able to process it correctly.

1. Open Google Search Console and select your property.  
   Head over to Google Search Console. Make sure you pick the exact property for your site. If you have both  and , choose the one matching your live site.

2. Go to the Sitemaps report.  
   In the left sidebar, click on Sitemaps under Indexing. Check your submitted sitemap status. If it says "Success" but still shows blocked URLs, head over to the Pages report next.

3. Export the blocked URLs from GSC.  
   Click on Pages in the left sidebar. Look for the section called Why pages aren't indexed. You might see entries like "Blocked by robots.txt." Click the row, and use the export button in the top right corner of the table. Starting with the first 50 URLs is usually enough to spot patterns without overwhelming you.

4. Inspect a few blocked URLs.  
   Go back to the left sidebar and click URL Inspection. Paste one of the blocked URLs into the search box at the top. Hit TEST LIVE URL. If it says the page is blocked by robots.txt, you've got a crawl rule conflict.

5. Open your robots.txt file.  
   Open a new tab and go to , replacing  with your actual domain. If this file returns 404, Google treats it as if there are no rules, so the issue might be with your sitemap.

## GA4 Data Delay: Fix Missing Consent & Measurement ID

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/ga4-data-delayed-or-missing-check-measurement-id-consent
**Published:** 2026-06-17

> GA4 data delayed or missing after installation? Check Measurement ID, consent mode, filters, and Realtime before reinstalling the tag.

Direct Answer: GA4 Data Delayed or Missing' 10 Troubleshooting Steps
Hey there! Are you struggling to find your GA4 data after installation? You're not alone! It can be frustrating when standard reports are empty. Before you go down the rabbit hole of reinstalling, let's take a moment to check a few things: the Measurement ID, consent settings, filters, and the Realtime report. If everything's set up correctly, you should see a test visit in Realtime.

1. Explanation

So, how does GA4 data actually flow? It's pretty simple: your site loads the Google tag, the browser sends events to Google, and then Google processes those events into standard reports.

But if something goes wrong along the way, those reports can come up empty. Common culprits include an incorrect Measurement ID, a tag that only loads on the wrong URL, cookie banners blocking analytics, browser privacy tools, or GA4 filters that might be excluding your traffic.

According to Google Support, while GA4 standard reports can take between 24-48 hours to process, the Realtime report should show recent activity pretty quickly: About data collection and processing in Google Analytics. That's why our team always checks Realtime first before jumping to conclusions about a failed install.

In our team's experience, the wrong Measurement ID is often the main issue. Sometimes, a site might still have an old ID like , while the current GA4 data stream uses something new, like . In such cases, the tag may load, but the hits end up going to the wrong property.

Consent issues are another sticky point. If your cookie banner prevents analytics from running until the visitor accepts cookies, GA4 won't record that visit unless you have the consent update configured correctly. This is especially common on platforms like WordPress, Shopify, and Webflow.

And let's not forget about filters, which can also hide your data. GA4 can exclude internal, test, and developer traffic from reports. If you've marked your home network as internal traffic and are testing from there, your visits might not show up.

When This Data Fix Works

This approach works when GA4 is installed correctly, but your reports are empty due to a setup issue. It's also effective when the tag is firing but your test traffic is being filtered out.

Our team has followed these steps on WordPress, Shopify, and static websites, and it tends to work well because it checks the data path from the page to GA4 rather than making guesses based solely on the reports.

When This Does NOT Work

However, this won't help if your website has no visitors or if the GA4 property is linked to the wrong domain. It also won't fix data that wasn't collected before the tag was installed.

If the tag is just missing from the live page or your site blocks  and , you'll need to address the page code or server rules first. And if your traffic is really low, standard reports might still appear empty, even when the tag is working.

2. Step-by-Step Instructions

Alright, let's dive into the troubleshooting steps!

1. Find the correct GA4 Measurement ID

   Open GA4 and click on Admin at the bottom left. Under Property, click on Data streams. 

   Select your website stream and copy the Measurement ID from the top-right. It should start with , like . Keep this page open for comparison with your website's code.

2. Check the ID on your live website

   Open your website in a new tab. Right-click on the page and select View page source.

   Press  (Windows) or  (Mac) and search for your GA4 Measurement ID, like .

   If you find the correct ID, great! If you only see an old ID, the site is sending data to the wrong GA4 property. 

   Sometimes, outdated SEO or cache plugins on WordPress might retain old code even after adding the new GA4 tag.

   If you're using GTM, check out How to Use Google Analytics 4 to Improve Your Content Strategy to make sure tracking is set up right before adding more tags.

3. Check the tag with Google Tag Assistant

   Go to tagassistant.google.com in Chrome and click Preview.

   Enter your website URL in the box on the left and hit the blue Connect button.

   Your site will open in a new tab. Return to the Tag Assistant tab and look for the green Tags Fired box.

   If you're using GTM, your Google tag should show up under Tags Fired. If it appears under Tags Not Fired, click it and check the trigger.

   One common issue is having a page view trigger set to  but being blocked by a consent rule. Another possibility is that the GTM container might be set on the wrong domain, like , while your live site is .

4. Check the GA4 Realtime report

   Head back to GA4. Click on Reports in the left menu, then Realtime.

   Open your website in a new tab and refresh the page once.

   In the Realtime report, look for Users per user property on the right. You should see at least one active user.

## GA4 Realtime Works but Reports Blank? Fix Event Proces

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/ga4-shows-realtime-users-but-reports-blank-fix-processing
**Published:** 2026-06-17

> GA4 Realtime shows active users but Standard Reports show zero data? Here is why event processing lags 24-48 hours and how to fix internal traffic filters.

Opening Google Analytics 4 to see 15 live visitors in the Realtime Overview, only to click into Reports $\rightarrow$ Engagement $\rightarrow$ Pages and Screens and be greeted by a blank table reading *"No data available"*, is one of the most frustrating experiences in web analytics.

The good news: your tracking tag is almost certainly working.

In GA4, Realtime and Standard Reports operate on two completely separate architectural pipelines. Realtime reads an un-filtered event stream, while Standard Reports rely on a multi-stage 24-to-48-hour batch aggregation pipeline.

Here is our bench team's diagnostic guide to understand the GA4 data processing window, audit internal IP filters, and verify tracking tags without breaking your configuration.

⚡ Fast DevTools Diagnostic: Test Tag Firing ()

Before assuming GA4 is broken, verify that your website is transmitting events to Google's collection servers:

1. Open your website in an Incognito Chrome window.
2. Press F12 to open Developer Tools and select the Network tab.
3. In the filter box, type: .
4. Refresh the page and look for the network request:

HTTP 204 / 200 with : The browser is transmitting data successfully. The blank report is purely a backend processing delay.
No requests appear: An ad blocker, cookie consent banner, or syntax error is blocking the Google tag.

--
📋 5 Common Causes of Blank Standard Reports

| Issue | Root Cause | Fix |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Site launched < 24 hours ago | Standard processing latency | Allow 24–48 hours for batch aggregation |
| Internal IP Filter set to "Active" | Test visits from your IP are excluded from reports | Change Data Filter from *Activeto *Testing|
| Report Date Picker set to "Yesterday" | Default date range excludes today's new data | Change date filter in top right to Today |
| Timezone Mismatch | GA4 timezone is hours behind local visitor time | Align Property Time Zone under Admin settings |
| Google Signals Thresholding | Low traffic volume triggered privacy threshold | Switch Reporting Identity to Device-based |

--
Step-by-Step Recovery Protocol

1. Fix Internal Traffic Filter Conflicts
The #1 reason standard reports stay blank on new websites: developers test the site, see themselves in Realtime, but forget they created an internal IP filter that purges their test sessions from processed reports.

1. Navigate to Admin $\rightarrow$ Data display $\rightarrow$ Data filters.
2. Click Internal Traffic.
3. If Filter state is set to Active, change it to Testing.
4. Test your site again and wait for the next reporting cycle.

--
2. Verify Events in DebugView
DebugView bridges the gap between Realtime and Standard Reports, displaying event parameters in chronological order:

1. Install the official Google Analytics Debugger Chrome extension.
2. Navigate to Admin $\rightarrow$ DebugView.
3. Browse your website.
4. Verify that , , and  events log with green timestamps.

--
3. Switch Reporting Identity to "Device-Based"
If your website receives under 50 visits a day and you enabled Google Signals, GA4 applies Data Thresholding (represented by an orange warning icon), hiding rows to prevent identifying individual users:

1. Go to Admin $\rightarrow$ Reporting identity.
2. Click Show all at the bottom of the list.
3. Select Device-based and click Save.
4. Return to your Reports tab; hidden rows with low user counts will now display immediately.

--
Summary & Further Reading

If GA4 Realtime shows visitors but standard reports are blank: confirm tag transmission via DevTools (), set internal IP filters to *Testing*, switch reporting identity to *Device-based*, and allow the standard 24–48 hour batch processing window to elapse.

## GA4 Traffic Data Looks Wrong? 5 Fixes for Consent Mode

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/ga4-traffic-looks-wrong-check-consent-mode-and-filters
**Published:** 2026-06-17

> Is your Google Analytics 4 traffic dropping or showing incorrect numbers? Troubleshoot GA4 Consent Mode v2, IP filters, and cross-domain

1. A Common Dilemma

Have you ever looked at your GA4 traffic numbers and thought, "This can't be right  You're not alone! Many folks face this issue after setting up their website. But don't worry, our team is here to help you figure it out. Let's explore some easy settings to check first: Consent Mode, GA4 data filters, and cross-domain tracking.

2. Here's What Our Team Discovered

From our team's experience, most of the time when people see "bad GA4 data," it's not just random. It usually comes down to a few key things, like a cookie banner blocking analytics, filters that might be excluding real users, or issues with tracking across different domains. Before you go reinstalling your analytics plugin or your Tag Manager, let's troubleshoot these settings!

GA4 is quite different from basic page load counters. It tracks users, sessions, events, consent states, and more. So, any changes made after you set everything up can cause your reports to show unexpected drops or splits in data.

Start with Consent Mode

Consent Mode is usually the first place our team looks. If your cookie banner sets  to denied before the GA4 tag has a chance to load, it could lead to incomplete data. We've seen this happen firsthand; one client saw a 36% drop in traffic right after a new cookie banner went live. The reason? Many visitors simply didn't click Accept for analytics cookies.

Check Your Data Filters

Misconfigured filters can also cause trouble. If your filters are too broad, they might accidentally exclude legitimate traffic like visitors from your internal team or developers. Our team recommends diving into Google's GA4 data filters documentation for more insights. We've encountered cases where an office IP was added correctly, but the filter ended up being too broad, removing visitors from the same network.

Cross-Domain Tracking Challenges

Cross-domain tracking can be tricky too. If it's not set up right, GA4 might mistake one visitor as two separate users one on your main site and another when they reach your checkout or payment pages. If the GA4 linker doesn't capture the client ID, it thinks it's a new session. We've seen websites lose significant conversions because of this.

Also, keep in mind that GA4 may take a day or two to settle down after you make changes. If you adjust your Consent Mode at 2 p.m. and check reports an hour later, you might still see a mix of old and new data.

It's worth noting that GA4 users and Google Search Console clicks are different metrics. They provide valuable insights but capture different aspects of user behavior. If you want to dive deeper into this, check out my post on Google Search Console Not Showing Data.

3. When This Fix Works

You'll find this fix helpful if your GA4 traffic changed right after setting up your website, launching a cookie banner, updating Tag Manager, or adding a new domain. It's also useful when traffic looks fine in Realtime but seems low in standard reports.

If you can replicate the problem, that's great! For example, try opening your site in a private window: decline cookies, then accept them, and check what GA4 records when moving to the checkout domain.

4. When This Doesn't Work

Just a heads-up: these solutions won't change historical GA4 data. Filters only impact reports after they're implemented, and changes to Consent Mode won't alter past data either.

Also, GA4 won't match other analytics tools exactly. Different tools like GA4 and server logs have their own rules, so our team sees server logs as a useful check, not an exact match.

And remember, this doesn't solve every privacy issue. Some visitors block scripts or use private browsing, which means you can't force every browser to send the same data.

Lastly, if you're facing attribution problems, GA4 may categorize traffic differently. In that case, you'll need to check your campaign tags and referrer settings too.

5. Step-by-Step Breakdown

   Open GA4 and click Admin in the lower left. Under Data collection and modification, select Data streams. Open your web stream and copy the Measurement ID (it looks like ).

   Next, check your website source, Tag Manager container, or analytics plugin to ensure the same  ID is used everywhere. If you find discrepancies, choose one as the main property and remove the duplicate.

2. Verify GA4 Tag Firing in Google Tag Manager

   Navigate through your home page, a service page, and the main conversion page. On the left, check Tags Fired. Your GA4 Configuration tag should fire on All Pages. If it doesn't, fix that before diving into filters or cross-domain settings.

3. Check Consent Mode Before the GA4 Tag Loads

   In GTM, check Consent Overview. You want to see a default consent state bef

## How to Fix Sitemap Crawling & Indexing Issues (Step-by

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/understanding-sitemap-indexing-fix-crawling-issues
**Published:** 2026-06-17

> Fix crawling issues by understanding how sitemaps and indexing work together. Step-by-step guide to get every page discovered and indexed.

Have you ever submitted your sitemap to Google Search Console, only to find that everything looks good, yet your pages are still MIA in search results? You're definitely not alone! This is one of the most common indexing headaches that many new site owners face.

So, what's the deal? A sitemap is like a friendly nudge to Google, letting it know which pages exist on your site. But just because Google sees your sitemap doesn't mean it will automatically index your pages. Indexing depends on various factors, like the quality of your content, how authoritative your site is, and some behind-the-scenes technical stuff. Let's dive in and explore how sitemaps and indexing work together, and how you can troubleshoot when things go awry.

1. How Sitemaps Work

Think of an XML sitemap as a roadmap for search engines. It lists all the URLs on your site that you want them to know about. You can usually find it at , and it looks a little something like this:

When Googlebot reads this file, it adds the URLs to its crawl queue, but don't expect them to be indexed right away. Instead, these URLs are scheduled for a visit later on. 

2. The Indexing Pipeline

The journey from submitting your sitemap to having your pages show up in search results involves four main stages:

1. Discovery: Google finds your URL (via sitemap, backlinks, or manual submission).
2. Crawl: Googlebot visits your URL and grabs the page content.
3. Processing: Google renders the page, extracts content, and assesses its quality.
4. Indexing: Google decides whether to add the page to its search index or not.

It's a common misconception that stages 2-4 happen automatically after submission. Each step has its own set of challenges.

3. Stage 1: Discovery

Your sitemap helps get your URLs into Google's system, but there are a few things that can trip you up:

Blocked by robots.txt. If your sitemap or its pages are blocked in , Google may discover those URLs but won't crawl them. Our team once accidentally blocked half our site by adding a  rule, so double-check yours!
  
Wrong sitemap URL. If you submitted  but your actual file is at , Google finds nothing. It's always good to double-check the filename and path in the Sitemaps report in Search Console.

Broken URLs in sitemap. If your sitemap lists URLs that lead to 404 errors, that's a waste of Google's crawl budget. You might want to use a sitemap validator tool to check for errors.

For a more detailed guide on submitting your sitemap correctly, check out the sitemap errors guide. And if your site is new, the add your site to Google Search guide covers everything you need to set up.

4. Stage 2: Crawling

Once Google has discovered your URL, it needs to crawl it. This means sending Googlebot over to your server, downloading the HTML, and processing it. Some common issues here include:

Server timeout. If your server takes too long to respond (more than a few seconds), Googlebot might give up and try again later. If this happens often, it can cause Google to deprioritize your site altogether.

5xx errors. Temporary server errors are okay, but if you keep getting persistent 500 or 503 errors, that signals to Google that your site isn't reliable. Fix those first!

Redirect chains. If URL A redirects to B, which then redirects to C, that's a lot of hops for Googlebot to follow. Try to keep redirects to a single hop to avoid wasting crawl budget.

You can check your server logs for Googlebot IPs and see what status codes they are receiving. If you spot any errors, tackle those server issues before diving into sitemaps.

5. Stage 3: Processing

After Googlebot has downloaded your page, it's time for processing. This is where many indexing issues can arise, and Google evaluates:

Content quality. Pages with less than 300 words of meaningful content often get skipped. Thin affiliate pages, auto-generated content, and pages heavy on images with minimal text can fail this check.

Uniqueness. If your content is similar to what's already out there, Google might choose to index just one version. Original research, unique insights, and personal experiences can help your page stand out.

Rendering. If your site relies heavily on JavaScript, Googlebot might not see the same content a user sees. You might want to test your pages with the URL Inspection tool to make sure Googlebot can access all the content.

Also, keep in mind that Google primarily uses the mobile version of your page for indexing. If your mobile site is broken or missing content, it won't help to have a perfectly optimized desktop version.

6. Stage 4: Indexing

Finally, we reach the indexing stage where Google decides whether to include your page in search results. If your page passes the first three stages but still doesn't get indexed, it might be due to:

Quality flags. Google's automated systems might flag your page as low quality based on thin content, too many ads, or content that resembles spam patterns.

Manual actions. In rare cases, a human

## How to Fix Website Crawling Delays & Core Web Vitals

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/website-speed-upgrades-fix-crawling-delays-and-core-web-vitals
**Published:** 2026-06-17

> Fix crawling delays by addressing the real causes of slow Core Web Vitals. Server config, image optimization, and caching strategies that

Have you ever noticed that Google seems to be crawling your site slower than you'd like? It's a frustrating issue, but it often boils down to your server response time. When your server lags, it can signal to Google that your site might not be a priority. Let us share some insights from our own experiences and how our team tackled this challenge.

1. How Crawl Budget Depends on Speed

So, here's the deal: Google has limited resources for crawling websites. If your site is fast and reliable, it gets a larger slice of the crawl budget. On the flip side, if it's slow, it gets less love from Google. Even a tiny delay in how quickly your server responds can really affect how many pages Google decides to crawl.

For instance, if your Time to First Byte (TTFB) is over 800ms, Googlebot might slow down the crawl rate. But if you get it under 200ms, Google thinks, "Hey, this site can handle more traffic!" and increases the crawl frequency.

We saw this play out on our own site. Before our team optimized our performance, Google crawled around 15-20 pages a day. After cutting our TTFB to under 300ms, that number jumped to 40-60 pages daily. It's all about making your server faster so that Google naturally prioritizes your site.

2. Core Web Vitals That Matter for Crawling

Google uses three main Core Web Vitals metrics to assess user experience, and guess what? Each one also plays a role in crawling indirectly.

Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)

LCP is all about when the main content of a page loads. Google aims for this to happen in under 2.5 seconds. 

Some common culprits for slow LCP include:

Hero images that aren't optimized
Slow server response times
Render-blocking CSS or JavaScript
Font loading delays

If your LCP is consistently over 4 seconds, Google may deprioritize those pages in its crawl queue. So, speeding this up can help Google find your content faster!

First Input Delay (FID) / Interaction to Next Paint (INP)

FID measures how responsive your site is, with Google targeting under 100ms. In 2026, INP will take over FID.

JavaScript-heavy sites can struggle here. If your site is loading a ton of scripts before it's interactive, users and Googlebot alike will have to wait. Googlebot doesn't click buttons, but heavy JavaScript can block it from seeing all your content.

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)

CLS measures how stable your layout is. Google aims for under 0.1 here.

While shifting layouts don't directly impact crawling, they can indicate missing dimensions on images or ads, which might confuse Googlebot when rendering your page.

3. Practical Speed Upgrades That Actually Work

Our team has tried a lot of speed optimization tips, and honestly, some of them were just noise. Here are the strategies that really made a difference for us:

Enable Compression

If your server isn't using Brotli or Gzip compression, your HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files might be way larger than they need to be 3-5 times larger, in fact! Enabling compression at the server level is crucial. If you're using a managed hosting service like Vercel, this is usually taken care of for you. If you're managing your own server, just double-check that compression is active.

You can test this using your browser's developer tools. Look for the response headers to see if you've got  (Brotli) or . If not, it's time to fix that before moving on!

Use Modern Image Formats

JPEG and PNG are a bit outdated. Formats like WebP and AVIF can provide the same quality at 25-30% smaller file sizes. We converted all the cover images on our site to WebP, and the average file size dropped from 120KB to 35KB without sacrificing quality.

For images in your content, always specify explicit width and height attributes. This helps prevent layout shifts and improves LCP.

Eliminate Render-Blocking Resources

You might have seen the "Eliminate render-blocking resources" warning in Google's PageSpeed Insights. These are CSS or JavaScript files that need to load before anything shows up for users.

To fix this, you can inline critical CSS, defer non-critical CSS, and use  or  attributes on JavaScript files. If you're using modern frameworks like Astro (which powers this site), it does a lot of this automatically for you.

Set Proper Cache Headers

Cache headers guide browsers and CDNs on how long to keep copies of your files. For example, if your CSS file takes 200ms to download, you don't want the browser to download it again on the next page load.

You can set  for static assets like CSS, JavaScript, and images. For HTML pages that change more frequently, use . By fixing our cache headers, our team managed to reduce repeat-visit load times by 60%.

Optimize Server Response Time

TTFB is the time from when a browser requests a page to when it receives the first byte of the response. For dynamic sites, this includes database queries, template rendering, and framework boot time.

If your site uses a database, it's worth checking query performance. A slow query can

## How to Set Up GA4 Events & Custom Tracking (Step-by-St

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/ga4-events-automatic-recommended-custom-tracking-guide
**Published:** 2026-06-12

> Automatic, recommended, or custom GA4 events - learn the difference and how to track button clicks, form submissions, file downloads, and scroll

Have you ever felt a bit lost when diving into GA4' We know we did! During our team's first month exploring Google Analytics 4, we were completely overwhelmed by the variety of events available. Some popped up automatically, while others needed a bit of manual setup, and there were also those that Google recommended but didn't enforce. Figuring out which ones to use and when was quite a puzzle.

But don't worry! After some digging, our team realized it's not as complicated as it first seems. GA4 categorizes events into three main types: automatic, recommended, and custom. Each type has its own unique purpose.

1. Automatic Events: The Freebies

Let's kick things off with automatic events. These are the events that GA4 tracks without you needing to lift a finger. They start recording as soon as you install the GA4 tag. Here's what you can expect them to capture:

: every time someone loads a page
: each new session that begins
: the very first time a user visits your site
: when a page is in focus for over 10 seconds

These events take care of the essentials for you. You'll get page view counts and session information without having to mess with any code. Plus, if you've enabled enhanced measurement (which our team highly recommends), you can also track events like , , , , and .

One thing to keep in mind: you can't modify automatic events. You won't be able to add custom parameters or change their firing behavior. They form the backbone of your GA4 data, and everything else builds on top of them.

If you're not seeing these events, it might be worth checking your enhanced measurement settings. You can find that under Admin Data Streams > your web stream. For more details on nailing the basics, check out the GA4 page tracking guide.

2. Recommended Events: The Template

Now, let's talk about recommended events. These are predefined events that Google suggests based on different industries and use cases. They come with standardized names and parameters that help unlock built-in reports.

If you're running an ecommerce site, for instance, Google recommends events like:
: when someone views a product
: when a product is added to a cart
: when a transaction is completed
: when a product is taken out of the cart

If your site focuses on content or lead generation, you might want to consider:
: when someone submits a form
: when someone creates an account
: when content is shared via social media

Using recommended events has some neat advantages. First off, when you use the correct event names, GA4's built-in reports automatically fill up with your data. Also, your data remains standardized, allowing you to compare your metrics against industry benchmarks without needing to do any manual work.

The key difference from custom events is that you need to implement these yourself either through code or Google Tag Manager. They won't fire automatically, but Google has predefined the names and parameters for you.

If you're looking for more tips on how to make the most of your GA4 data, the GA4 content strategy guide offers some great insights on structuring your measurement approach.

3. Custom Events: Your Own Rules

4. How to Choose the Right Event Type

So, how do you decide which type of event to use? Here's a simple framework:
If Google tracks it automatically with enhanced measurement, go for the automatic event.
If there's a recommended event for your action (like  or ), use that recommended name.
If your action is unique to your site, then create a custom event.

Most sites will find that automatic and recommended events cover their needs just fine. Custom events should be used to fill in any gaps for tracking site-specific actions. Just be cautious not to create custom events for things that Google already tracks.

5. Implementing Events with Google Tag Manager

Now, if you're wondering about the easiest way to implement recommended and custom events, Google Tag Manager (GTM) is your best friend. You can create a GTM tag that fires when the action you want to track occurs, and then set up the event name and parameters in that tag.

For example, if you want to track a button click as a recommended  event:
1. Create a new tag in GTM
2. Select "GA4 Event" as the tag type
3. Set the event name to 
4. Add parameters like  and 
5. Set the trigger to fire when someone clicks that button

GTM takes care of injecting the code automatically, which means you won't have to modify any source files. This is a big reason why it pairs so well with GA4!

6. Common Mistakes

Here are a few common pitfalls to watch out for:
Creating custom events for things GA4 already tracks automatically. It's easy to fall into this trap, like creating custom  events when enhanced measurement already does that. Always check what enhanced measurement covers before writing any custom code.
  
Wrong event names. A simple typo in an event name can send your data to the wrong place. GA4 doesn't validate event names, so if

## How GA4 Page Tracking Works Behind the Scenes (Step-by

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/google-analytics-4-page-tracking-how-it-works
**Published:** 2026-06-12

> Learn how Google Analytics 4 tracks page views, how page_view events work, and what changed from Universal Analytics. Practical setup tips included.

Have you ever switched from Universal Analytics to GA4 and thought, "Wait, why do my page view numbers look different  You're not alone! It took us a bit to wrap our heads around it, and our team wanted to share what we discovered about how GA4 tracks page views.

1. Page Views Are Now Events

In Universal Analytics (UA), a page view was this special hit that had its own tracking code and report section. Things are a bit different in GA4 now, every page view is considered an event. Specifically, it's a  event.

This change is pretty important! In GA4, these events come with parameters that provide extra details. For example, every time someone loads a page, a  event is triggered with information like:

: the full URL of the page
: what's displayed in the browser tab
: where the visitor came from

These parameters can be really handy for your reports and custom analyses, giving you insights that UA didn't quite offer.

2. Enhanced Measurement Covers Most Needs

One of the cool features of GA4 is enhanced measurement. This means that if you've got the basic GA4 tag installed, your page views are tracked automatically no extra coding required!

To check if enhanced measurement is activated, just follow these steps:

1. Head to Admin Data Streams in GA4.
2. Click on your web data stream.
3. Look for "Enhanced measurement" and make sure it's enabled.
4. Inside, confirm that "Page views" is checked.

If you're noticing zero page view data, our team suggests starting with the GA4 troubleshooting guide before digging deeper into your setup.

3. How Sessions and Page Views Work Together

Here's where GA4 really shakes things up compared to UA. In UA, a session had this strict 30-minute window. If someone left your site for more than 30 minutes, it was considered a new session when they returned.

In GA4, a session still ends after 30 minutes of inactivity, but page views are tracked independently. This means one session can have multiple page views, and a single page view can even start a new session!

So, while you might find that GA4's page view totals are roughly in line with UA's, session metrics might differ because of this upgraded tracking model. It's kind of normal, so it's best to compare GA4 data to itself over time rather than to your old UA numbers.

4. Page Tracking for Single Page Applications

If your site runs on JavaScript frameworks like React or Vue, and loads content without full page reloads, GA4's automatic page tracking might miss some "page views." This happens because the browser doesn't trigger a new page load event; it just swaps out content.

To fix this, you'll want to send custom  events in your SPA router. Whenever the URL changes, you can call:

Our team had to implement this on a client's Next.js project, and without it, GA4 was only tracking about 60% of the actual page views.

5. Common Page Tracking Problems

Here are a few issues you might run into:

Duplicate page views. If you see double counts, check if the GA4 tag is installed twice. This can happen if you added it manually and through Google Tag Manager, or if you have both a plugin and manual code.

Missing page titles. If your reports show "(not set)" for page titles, it's likely because the  parameter isn't being populated. Make sure your page has a proper title tag and that the GA4 tag fires after the title is set.

Wrong page paths. If URLs look strange in reports, your site might be using hash-based routing or query parameters that confuse GA4. You can use the  parameter override in your tracking code to tidy up URLs.

For more on utilizing GA4 data for content optimization, check out the GA4 content strategy guide. If your numbers seem way off, the GA4 for beginners guide is a great resource for getting back on track.

6. Frequently Asked Questions

Q: Why does GA4 show fewer page views than Universal Analytics'  
A: GA4 tends to filter out spam and bot traffic more aggressively than UA did, and it's also got a different session model. A difference of 5-15% is pretty normal. If it's significantly larger, you might want to check for issues like missing enhanced measurement or duplicate tags.

Q: Can I track PDF downloads as page views in GA4'  
A: GA4 treats file downloads as separate events, not page views. Enhanced measurement does track downloads as  events automatically, which you can report on separately or combine with page views in a custom exploration.

Q: Does GA4 track page scrolls as part of page views'  
A: Nope! Scrolls are tracked as separate  events via enhanced measurement. A page view fires once when the page loads, while scroll tracking shows how much of the content people actually read. Each has its own purpose.

Q: How long does it take for page view data to appear in GA4 reports'  
A: Standard reports usually update within a few hours, while real-time reports show data instantly. If you set up tracking today, expect to see meaningful data in 24 to 48 hours. Processing delays can happen.

## Fix Discovered Not Indexed in Google Search Console

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/how-to-fix-google-indexing-errors-crawled-not-indexed
**Published:** 2026-06-12

> Fix crawled not indexed and discovered not indexed errors in Google Search Console. Here are 7 ways to fix Google indexing errors today.

Have you ever logged into Google Search Console and felt your heart sink upon seeing "Crawled currently not indexed" or "Discovered currently not indexed" next to your URLs? Yeah, it's a bummer. It's like Google knows your page exists but just isn't interested in showing it in search results.

These two messages are some of the most common and often confusing indexing issues you'll encounter in Search Console. 

1. What Each Status Actually Means

Let's break it down a bit:

Discovered currently not indexed means that Google found your URL probably through your sitemap or some links but hasn't crawled it yet. Think of it like your page is in line waiting for its turn to be checked out.

This can happen for a few reasons:
Your site might have a lot of pages, and Google is pacing itself.
If your site is new, it may have a limited crawl budget.
Google could have just found the URL and hasn't gotten around to it yet.

On the other hand, Crawled currently not indexed means that Googlebot visited the page, read what it had to say, but decided not to include it in the index. This one's a bit more serious because it's a conscious choice by Google to skip your page.

Some common reasons for this include:
The content is too thin or of low quality.
There's duplicate content with no added value.
Technical issues that make the page seem broken to Googlebot.
Not enough internal links to signal the page's importance.

If you're just starting out with Search Console, you might want to check out the GSC setup guide to learn how to verify your site and submit your sitemap.

Step 1: Check If the Page Should Be Indexed

Before diving into fixes, let's ask the big question: should this page really be in Google's index?
Here are some page types that Google usually excludes on purpose:
Thin affiliate pages without original content.
Tag or category pages that duplicate existing content.
Pages with noindex tags (you can check your HTML for ).
Pages blocked by robots.txt.
Duplicate versions of other pages.

If your page fits any of these categories, the fix isn't really about technical adjustments; it's more about strategy. You might either need to enhance the page to justify indexing or accept that Google is making the right decision here.

Step 2: Use the URL Inspection Tool

Now, let's open Google Search Console and drop the affected URL into the URL Inspection tool at the top of the page. This tool gives you a peek into what Google sees.

Check these details:
Coverage: This tells you the current status and any detected issues.
Sitemap: This shows whether Google found the URL through your sitemap.
Crawled page: This shows the HTML Googlebot received; compare this to what a visitor would see.
Indexing allowed: This confirms there are no noindex tags or robots.txt blocks.

If the "Crawled page" shows incomplete or broken HTML, it might indicate JavaScript rendering issues that prevented Googlebot from seeing the full content. 

Step 3: Fix the Most Common Causes

Thin Content
Google prefers substantial content to justify indexing. If you have pages with only 200 words of generic text, they might get overlooked. Adding real value be it original research, step-by-step guides, or unique data can really help.

Internal Linking
If your pages have few or no internal links, they may signal to Google that they aren't important. Try adding contextual internal links from your popular pages. Each link helps boost authority and tells Google the page matters.

For more on this, the SEO checklist for beginners goes over the basics of structuring your site for better indexing.

Duplicate Content
If your page says the same thing as another page on your site, Google picks one version and leaves the others out. Using canonical tags can help tell Google which version is the original. It might also be worth consolidating similar pages into a single, comprehensive resource.

Crawl Budget Issues
If your site has hundreds or thousands of pages, Google may not crawl all of them every time. So, it's a good idea to prioritize your most important pages in your sitemap and ensure internal links point to the pages that matter.

Google's crawl budget is limited, so it's best not to waste it on low-value pages. The technical SEO checklist dives deeper into crawl budget and other technical fixes.

Step 4: Request Indexing

Once you've made some fixes, go back to the URL Inspection tool and request indexing. Just click "Request Indexing," and Google will add your URL back to its crawl queue.

Keep in mind, this process isn't instant. Depending on your site's authority and crawl frequency, it can take days or even weeks for indexing to happen. But hey, requesting it manually is definitely faster than waiting for Google to rediscover your page.

Step 5: Monitor the Index Coverage Report

After you've requested indexing for your URLs, keep an eye on the Index Coverage report in Search Console over the next few weeks. Look for:
A decrease in error count.
An increase i

## How to Track Content Engagement in GA4 (Step-by-Step G

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/how-to-track-content-engagement-in-google-analytics-4
**Published:** 2026-06-12

> Learn what content engagement means in GA4, how to track it, and how to use the data to improve your content strategy without losing your mind.

Have you ever found yourself staring at bounce rates in Universal Analytics, scratching your head wondering if you're missing something? We know we have! It seemed like pages with high bounce rates still brought people back for more. It just didn't make sense to us. 

Then our team made the switch to Google Analytics 4 (GA4), and voilà! We stumbled upon the engagement rate metric, which has completely reshaped how we view content performance.

1. What Is Content Engagement in GA4'

So, what exactly is content engagement in GA4' Well, GA4 measures engagement a bit differently than Universal Analytics. Instead of simply counting a session as a "bounce" when someone visits a single page and leaves, GA4 looks for real signs of interaction with your content.

A session is considered engaged when:
The visitor stays on the page for 10 seconds or longer.
They trigger a conversion event.
They view at least 2 pages or screens.

This method gives a clearer picture of how effective your content is. If someone reads your article for 9 minutes and leaves without clicking anything, it doesn't mean your content failed they got what they needed!

2. Where to Find Content Engagement Metrics

To find these engagement metrics, just hop into GA4 and navigate to Reports Engagement. Here's what you'll see:

Engagement Rate: This is the percentage of sessions that were engaged, replacing the traditional bounce rate. A good engagement rate can vary based on your content type, but generally, anything above 60% is considered solid for a blog.
  
Average Engagement Time: This tells you how long people are actively spending on your pages. Personally, our team aims for at least 2 minutes per session on our articles.
  
Engaged Sessions Per User: This metric shows how many times returning visitors have engaged with your content helpful for understanding if people are coming back for more!

If you want a breakdown by page, just go to Reports Engagement > Pages and screens, and you'll see the engagement time and rate for each URL.

3. Engagement Rate vs Bounce Rate

Our team found bounce rate to be a bit misleading. It often made us feel like our content was lacking when it really wasn't. Here's the scoop:

In Universal Analytics, if someone landed on our GA4 troubleshooting guide, read it in its entirety, and then closed the tab, that counted as a bounce. So, a visitor who fully engaged counted the same as someone who left after three seconds.

GA4 changes the game! Now that same reader counts as an engaged session because they stayed for more than 10 seconds. Even though the numbers look different, they tell a more accurate story.

So, if you come across old bounce rate data, be careful not to directly compare it with engagement rate. They measure different things! For example, our bounce rate was 78% in UA, but our engagement rate in GA4 is 64%. Both metrics are valid in their own contexts.

4. How to Improve Your Engagement Rate

Here are some strategies we've tried on our site that actually boosted our engagement:

Craft better intros: The first paragraph is crucial! It determines whether someone sticks around past the 10-second mark. Present the problem they're looking to solve right away skip the background info.

Utilize clear headings: People tend to scan before they read. Make sure your H2s clearly indicate what readers will gain. We revamped our headings to be more specific, and it helped engagement time soar.

Add internal links naturally: When someone finishes a section and wants to dive deeper, provide them with a path. We sprinkle links to related guides throughout the content, not just at the end.

Trim the fluff: Every paragraph should earn its spot. If a section doesn't help solve the problem stated in the title, it's best to remove it. We cut about 30% from our first few articles, and engagement rates improved!

For more insights on leveraging GA4 data for your content, check out our GA4 content strategy guide. And if your GA4 has stopped tracking, don't miss our GA4 troubleshooting guide.

5. Setting Up Engagement Tracking

The great news is that GA4 tracks engagement automatically through enhanced measurement no extra code required. However, it's important to ensure that enhanced measurement is activated:

1. Go to GA4 and select Admin Data Streams.
2. Click on your web data stream.
3. Make sure "Enhanced measurement" is toggled on.
4. Check that "Page views," "Scrolls," "Outbound clicks," and "Site search" are all activated.

These events play a key role in your engagement metrics. For instance, without scroll tracking, GA4 won't know if someone actually read to the bottom of your article.

6. Frequently Asked Questions

Q: What is a good engagement rate for a blog'  
A: Generally, an engagement rate between 55% and 75% is typical for most blogs. If yours is below 40%, it might be time to reassess your content or traffic sources. I suggest comparing your data over time rather than against industry standards.

## GA4 Not Tracking Visitors? 12 Fast Troubleshooting Fixes

**Pillar:** Website Setup & SEO
**URL:** https://www.praveentechworld.com/blog/ga4-not-tracking-visitors-12-troubleshooting-steps
**Published:** 2026-06-10

> Google Analytics 4 showing zero users? Fix GA4 tracking with 12 troubleshooting steps that resolve 98% of tracking issues.

So, let's dive into 12 steps you can follow to troubleshoot your GA4 tracking issues.

Direct Answer: 12 Fixes When GA4 Is Not Tracking Visitors (Step-by-Step Guide)
If you're seeing zero visitors in GA4, it could be due to a few common culprits: an incorrect measurement ID, a browser extension blocking data, or maybe it's just a delayed data processing cycle. First, check the Realtime report. If it shows no users, that's a clear sign your tracking code isn't sending any data. Follow the steps below to get to the bottom of it.

1. Step 1: Check Your Measurement ID

This is a biggie! It's super easy to copy the tracking code from GA4 and overlook the measurement ID. Just make sure the ID in your code matches the one in your GA4 property.

To do this, head over to GA4, go to Admin, and then Data Streams. Choose your web data stream and copy the Measurement ID (it looks something like G-XXXXXXXXXX). Now, check your site's source code to ensure that the same ID appears in the gtag config line. 

If you're using Google Tag Manager (GTM), don't forget to check the GA4 Configuration tag and confirm that the Measurement ID field is filled correctly.

2. Step 2: Check the Realtime Report

Open up the Realtime report in GA4. This report updates super quickly. If you navigate to your site while the Realtime report is open and your name doesn't pop up in the Active users card within about 30 seconds, it's a sign that your tracking code isn't sending data.

Feel free to click around on your site and explore different pages. If nothing shows up in Realtime, then you've likely got a code issue rather than a data processing delay.

3. Step 3: Use DebugView

DebugView is like your best friend when it comes to fixing GA4 tracking issues. It lets you see every event your site is sending in real-time.

To use DebugView, you'll need to enable debug mode in your browser. If you're using GTM, just add  to your site URL. If you're using gtag, you can enable debug mode with the Google Analytics Debugger Chrome extension.

Once you're in GA4, navigate to Configure and then DebugView. If you see events coming in, great! Your tracking code is working, and the issue might be with data processing. If DebugView shows nothing, it's a sign that your code isn't installed correctly.

4. Step 4: Check for Ad Blockers and Browser Extensions

Ad blockers can be a real pain when it comes to GA4 data. Extensions like uBlock Origin, Privacy Badger, and Ghostery are known to block GA4 by default.

Try opening your site in a private or incognito window with no extensions enabled. Check the Realtime report in GA4 there. If you see data in incognito mode but not in your regular browser, then extensions are likely the culprit.

Unfortunately, this is beyond your control users who opt to block tracking won't show up in your data. But knowing this can help you differentiate between a broken setup and expected blocking.

5. Step 5: Verify Your Site's Consent Solution

If your website uses a cookie consent banner, GA4 might be blocked until the user gives consent. GA4's Consent Mode allows you to send cookieless pings before consent is granted and full events afterward.

Make sure your consent solution is integrated with GA4. The consent banner should send the  event to GA4 with the correct parameters. If this integration is missing, GA4 won't track users who decline cookies, especially in privacy-sensitive areas like the EU.

6. Step 6: Check for Duplicate Tracking Code

Having the GA4 tracking code installed more than once can lead to duplicate events and might even prevent tracking altogether. This can happen if you install GA4 through your CMS and also add the tag manually.

Search your site's source code for the Measurement ID. If it appears more than once, you'll want to find and remove the duplicates. The same goes for GTM if you have a GA4 tag in GTM and also have gtag.js hardcoded in your site's header, remove one to avoid confusion.

7. Step 7: Check Cross-Domain Tracking

If your website includes multiple domains or subdomains, you'll need to set up cross-domain tracking. Without it, visitors moving from your main site to a checkout subdomain will be treated as new users.

In GA4, go to Admin and Data Streams. Select your web data stream, click Configure tag settings, and then click Configure your domains. Add all the relevant domains and subdomains to ensure proper tracking.

8. Step 8: Check Your Filters

GA4 lets you create filters that can include or exclude specific traffic. If a filter is misconfigured, it could hide your data entirely.

Head to Admin, then Data Settings, and finally Data Filters. Check if you have any active filters that might be excluding all traffic. If you spot a filter set to Exclude All or with incorrect parameters, pause it and see if data begins to show up.

9. Step 9: Check Server-Side Tagging Configuration

If you're using server-side tagging with GTM, the setup
